That said, irregular activities and espionage seem to be on the uptick in the region, particularly around the flashpoints of the North Atlantic–Barents Sea area as opposed to the North Pacific, Bering, and Chukchi Seas area. This is evidenced by instances such as the unexplained January 2022 cutting of deep-sea cables between Svalbard and the Norwegian mainland, the potential cutting of cables in the Gulf of Finland by a Chinese container ship, Newnew Polar Bear, that had traversed the Northern Sea Route in 2023 (Humpert 2023), Russia's weaponization of migrants, whom it forced upon Finland at the border, leading Helsinki to close its border with Russia (Moshes 2023), and an alleged Russian spy employed as a researcher at the University of Tromsø and arrested there (Cecco 2022).

Proxy Conflict: Greenland. Very small countries can become a target of proxy geopolitical conflict when not clearly aligned and especially if their domestic political systems are unstable, with competing parties inviting outside aid and intervention. Two contemporary examples are the Solomon Islands (where Australia and the United States have been engaged in a proxy conflict with China) and the Maldives (where India and China compete for influence). If Greenland does become fully independent from the Kingdom of Denmark, it will be a geostrategically important country with ample unexploited mineral resources, and a small, majority-Indigenous population of 57,000. Already in the late 2010s, as Chinese actors offered to develop Greenlandic minerals and build the international airports the Greenlandic home-rule government wanted, Washington stepped in to ensure continued western dominance of the island (Szymański 2021). Donald Trump's 2019 quixotic and anachronistic suggestion to buy Greenland from Denmark was made in this context.

Foreign policy and defense have not been transferred to the Greenlandic self-rule government, but Greenland seeks to chart its own path in these areas. For the present, Greenland appears quite firmly within the Western orbit, bound to it by strategic interests, values, and the nature of its political system. The EU has followed the US in establishing a presence in Nuuk. In February 2024, the Greenlandic parliamentary majority parties released a foreign, defense, and security policy strategy to 2033, “Nothing About Us Without Us,” that backs Greenland's continued engagement with western institutions such as NATO, seeks strengthened relations with North America (including its Arctic Indigenous peoples), and expresses the country's desire that the Arctic remain a region of low tension under the rule of law (Breum 2024; Jacobsen and Rahbek-Clemmensen 2024; Government of Greenland 2024).
